questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What viscosity does to flow through a pipe
questions.learningObjective: Identify how viscosity changes the pressure drop needed for a given flow
questions.stem: A design brief asks how a viscous oil behaves when it is pumped along a long, narrow feed line under a fixed pump pressure. What is the main effect of viscosity on the flow?

options.text: The flow rate falls as viscosity rises, because greater internal friction resists the motion of the oil
options.misconception: believes viscosity changes only the appearance of the oil

options.text: The flow rate rises as viscosity rises, because the oil becomes easier to move once the pump warms it
options.misconception: confuses viscosity with temperature

options.text: The pressure drop needed to drive a given flow grows with viscosity, so more pumping power is required
Viscosity has no effect on the pressure drop, since the pipe diameter alone sets the resistance
options.misconception: believes pipe diameter is the only source of flow resistance

questions.explanation: Viscous fluids resist shear, so a bigger pressure gradient is needed to push the same flow through a pipe. Diameter matters too, but denying any role for viscosity confuses one part with the whole.
questions.hint: Think of oil compared with treacle flowing through a tube.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Terminal speed as a balance of two forces
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the terminal speed of a falling body from the balance of weight and drag
questions.stem: A steel ball of mass 0.010 kg falls through oil whose drag force is 0.20 newtons per metre per second of speed, with buoyancy neglected. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared and give the terminal speed in metres per second.
questions.explanation: At terminal speed the drag equals the weight, so kv = mg and v = mg/k. Here v = 0.010 x 9.8 divided by 0.20 = 0.49 m/s, and multiplying by the drag constant rather than dividing is the usual slip.
questions.hint: Set the drag force equal to the weight.

questions.stem: A design brief asks why a steel needle can rest on the surface of a bowl of water without sinking. Which explanation of surface tension is correct?

options.text: Cohesive forces between water molecules pull the surface into a film that resists stretch, holding the needle
The water surface acts like a stretched rubber sheet whose tension is set by the depth of the bowl
options.misconception: treats the surface as a solid membrane, not a film

options.text: Air pressure above the needle is greater than the pressure below it, so the needle is held up by the air
options.misconception: confuses air pressure with surface tension

options.text: The needle is buoyant because the water displaced under it equals its weight
options.misconception: mistakes buoyancy for the cause of surface tension support

questions.explanation: Surface tension is cohesion between surface molecules, so the film resists stretching and can carry a needle. The rubber-sheet idea is only an analogy, and buoyancy plays no part.
questions.hint: Think about what holds molecules together at the surface.

options.misconception: believes viscosity and density are the same property

options.text: The drop is explained by the pipe being longer, since viscosity can never influence a pipeline's flow
options.misconception: denies any connection between viscosity and flow rate

options.text: A more viscous oil shears more readily at the walls, so the same pump pressure pushes less oil through
The drop is explained by the oil cooling, since cooler oil always flows faster than warm oil

questions.topic: Terminal speed as a balance of two forces

questions.stem: Two stages of a brief ask: first, find the drag constant implied by a 0.050 kg sphere that settles at 0.98 m/s in a fluid, then state the terminal speed of a 0.100 kg sphere in the same fluid. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared. What is the second-stage answer?

options.text: 0.49 m/s, because the second stage simply halves the first-stage speed
options.misconception: divides by two without the stage one constant

options.text: 0.98 m/s, because the terminal speed of a sphere never depends on its mass
options.misconception: believes terminal speed is independent of the falling mass

options.text: 3.92 m/s, because terminal speed scales with the square of the mass in a linear drag law
options.misconception: applies a quadratic relationship where linear drag is given

options.text: 1.96 m/s, because the drag constant is 0.50 and doubling the mass doubles the terminal speed

questions.explanation: Stage one gives k = mg/v = 0.50, and stage two gives v = mg/k = 1.96 m/s. With linear drag the speed is proportional to mass, so the correct figure is a doubling rather than a halving or a squaring.
questions.hint: Find k in stage one before using it in stage two.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a floating body sits lower in salt water than in fresh water
questions.learningObjective: Explain the change of draught when a vessel moves from river to sea
questions.stem: A written explanation is asked for of what happens to a ship that moves from a river into sea water, and what a loading master must check about the change in buoyancy.

answer.exemplar: A floating ship must displace a weight of water equal to its own, so in the denser sea water it needs a smaller displaced volume and rises slightly higher in the water. The loading master should check the new draught and the under-keel clearance, and note that the margin on the buoyancy has changed even though the cargo has not.

questions.explanation: In denser sea water the same weight needs less displaced volume, so the ship floats higher and its draught shrinks. Saying the sea pushes it up more misses the falling displacement.
questions.hint: Weigh the displaced liquid, not the depth.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What viscosity does to flow through a pipe
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the pressure drop along a pipe from the viscosity and flow speed
questions.stem: A design brief requires oil of density 900 kg per cubic metre to flow through a horizontal pipe of length 50 m and diameter 0.04 m. Using the relation dP = 32 mu L v over d squared with viscosity 0.10 Pa s and speed 1.0 m/s, calculate the pressure drop in pascals.
questions.explanation: Substituting gives dP = 32 x 0.10 x 50 x 1.0 over 0.0016 = 100000 Pa. Forgetting to square the diameter, or dropping the factor of 32, gives a very different answer.
questions.hint: The diameter appears squared in the denominator.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Terminal speed as a balance of two forces
questions.learningObjective: Identify what information is missing before a terminal speed claim can be checked
questions.stem: A design brief claims that a falling sphere in oil reaches a steady speed of 3.0 m/s, and a colleague objects that the number cannot be checked. Which criticism is the strongest?

options.text: The claim is impossible, because a sphere in a liquid always accelerates until it reaches the tank floor
options.misconception: believes falling bodies never reach a steady speed

options.text: The claim is impossible, because terminal speed only exists for objects falling through air
options.misconception: confines terminal speed to air, not any fluid

options.text: The claim is weak, because terminal speeds are always the same for spheres of a given size
options.misconception: thinks sphere size alone fixes the terminal speed

options.text: The claim gives no drag constant or sphere mass, and terminal speed cannot be found without them

questions.explanation: Terminal speed comes from balancing weight against drag, so the mass and drag constant are needed before any number can be checked. Saying spheres never settle is wrong.
questions.hint: Ask which two quantities the balance of forces requires.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What surface tension is
questions.learningObjective: Find the mass a floating needle can be supported by at a known surface tension
questions.stem: A needle brief works in two stages: it first finds the force a water surface can exert on a 0.30 m needle using a surface tension of 0.072 newtons per metre and two contact lines, then finds the mass that force can support. Take g as 9.8 m/s squared. What are the two answers?

options.text: 0.0216 N then 0.00220 kg, because only one contact line carries the needle
options.misconception: counts only one contact line on the liquid surface

options.text: 0.0432 N then 0.00441 kg, because two contact lines share the load
0.0432 N then 0.43 N, because the mass is found by multiplying the force by gravity
options.misconception: confuses mass with weight and the working direction

options.text: 0.0144 N then 0.00147 kg, because the surface tension applies three times over
options.misconception: invents a third contact line for a single floating needle

questions.explanation: Stage one gives F = 2 x 0.072 x 0.30 = 0.0432 N, and stage two gives m = F divided by g = 0.00441 kg. Counting one line, or multiplying by gravity, misstates the calculation.
questions.hint: Count both contact lines, then divide the force by gravity.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a manometer compares
questions.learningObjective: Choose the manometer arrangement that reads the gauge pressure of a pipe
questions.stem: One design brief asks how a manometer on a pipe is arranged so that the instrument reads the pressure difference and not some other quantity. Which arrangement is correct?

options.text: One limb connects to the pipe and the other is open to the atmosphere, so the height gives the gauge pressure
Both limbs connect to the pipe at different points, so the difference between them is the pressure difference
options.misconception: confuses a two-point manometer with this one

options.text: Both limbs are sealed and evacuated, so the liquid levels show the absolute pressure of the pipe
options.misconception: believes an evacuated limb can show the absolute pressure

options.text: One limb is connected to the pipe and the other to a vacuum, so the height gives the absolute pressure
options.misconception: claims an evacuated limb measures absolute pressure

questions.explanation: With one limb on the pipe and the other open to the atmosphere, the level difference gives the gauge pressure. Two connected limbs compare two points, and an evacuated limb is not usable.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two limbs is open to the atmosphere.
